name: Adivasi in India
region: Central India — Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh; tiger reserve states
summary: In June 2024, India's National Tiger Conservation Authority ordered the forced relocation of 89,800 tribal families from 848 villages in 54 tiger reserves — potentially one of the largest conservation-driven displacements ever ordered. An estimated 30 million Adivasi have been displaced since independence. 104.3 million Adivasi (8.6% of India's population) face ongoing dispossession, criminalization, and exclusion.
context:
India's 104.3 million Adivasi (Scheduled Tribes, also called Indigenous or tribal peoples) are among the country's most marginalized populations, facing systematic dispossession, discrimination, and exclusion from the development and conservation processes that directly affect their lands and lives.

The June 2024 NTCA order — directing the forced relocation of 89,800 tribal families from 848 villages in 54 tiger reserves — represents one of the most dramatic recent examples of what critics call 'fortress conservation': the displacement of Indigenous peoples in the name of wildlife protection. International experts and Indigenous rights organizations have described this potential displacement as possibly the largest ever undertaken under the banner of conservation. Research consistently shows that areas managed by Indigenous communities have better conservation outcomes than those managed by state exclusion.

An estimated 30 million Adivasi have been displaced from their ancestral lands since India's independence in 1947 — by dams, mines, national parks, military zones, and industrial projects. The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act of 2006 was intended to address this history of dispossession, but implementation has been systematically undermined.

Adivasi communities also face violence. In Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, military and paramilitary operations targeting Maoist insurgents have resulted in documented abuses against tribal civilians — arbitrary detention, torture, destruction of villages, and killings. The conflation of Adivasi identity with Maoist sympathies has been used to justify violence and criminalization.

Forest rights activists — those working to implement the Forest Rights Act — face UAPA charges, arrests, and in some cases killing. The criminalization of Indigenous forest rights defense is a persistent pattern.

awareness: Share that 89,800 tribal families were ordered evicted from tiger reserves in 2024 — this is conservation-driven displacement on a potentially historic scale
Highlight the research consensus: Indigenous-managed territories have better conservation outcomes than fortress conservation — evicting Adivasi doesn't save tigers, it removes forest guardians
Amplify Adivasi activists, academics, and journalists fighting for forest rights implementation and against criminalization of Indigenous land defense
Raise awareness about the 30 million displaced since independence — dam, mine, and park displacement is a structural pattern, not an exception
Challenge corporations whose supply chains depend on mines, plantations, and projects built on Adivasi land without free, prior, and informed consent
political: Urge the Indian government to implement rather than undermine the Forest Rights Act — communities with recognized forest rights cannot be evicted without their consent
Advocate for India to halt the NTCA relocation order and conduct meaningful consultation with affected tribal communities
Push for independent investigations into paramilitary abuses against Adivasi communities in conflict-affected states
Support calls for India to adopt UNDRIP (UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples) into domestic law
Demand that development finance institutions (World Bank, ADB) make Free, Prior and Informed Consent a binding condition for all projects affecting Adivasi communities
